title: Snail and parasite identification
text:
Schistosomiasis surveys depend on telling snail species apart, and on spotting the human parasite among the many look-alike larvae that snails release. Both take trained experts, who are scarce in the places that need them.
I co-developed deep learning models that identify medically important snails and parasite larvae from microscope and field photos taken in Senegal. They performed about as well as experienced parasitologists, and the labeled images were released for others to use.



I’m now leading a new version with the De Leo lab, adding snails from Côte d’Ivoire and Brazil.
Papers: Tallam et al. 2021, Frontiers in Public Health
Figure from Tallam et al. 2021, CC BY.

title: Snail habitat from space, Senegal River basin
text:
Dams and irrigation along the Senegal River changed its water and fed the plants that schistosomiasis snails live in. Surveys on foot reach only a few sites; the risk spreads across the whole basin.
We built a deep learning model that maps floating plants, rooted plants, open water and land from high-resolution satellite images, using drone maps and field surveys to teach it what each looks like from above. I helped build, train and test the model, organized the image data, labeled the training maps and led the drone mapping behind them. The approach grew into an AI platform for mapping schistosomiasis risk from space.



Papers: Liu et al. 2022, Remote Sensing
News: Stanford HAI, March 2020 · Stanford Report, March 2026 · Stanford HAI, March 2026

title: Mosquito breeding sites: Indonesia, Kenya, Costa Rica
text:
Discarded tires and trash collect rainwater and are some of the most productive breeding sites for the mosquito that spreads dengue. Finding them on foot is slow and misses many.

Indonesia: I trained the deep learning model that finds tires in drone imagery of Makassar, and I take the imagery from raw drone photos to finished maps. I’m now building the next model, which sorts trash piles into types as well as finding tires.
Kenya: the same group built a way to spot trash piles and tires in drone images and checked it against surveys on foot.
Costa Rica: I planned drone flights in two regions and lead the analysis: testing whether our tire model works in towns it was never trained on, and scaling drone maps up to satellite imagery.




Papers: Hassan, Chamberlin et al. 2026, Remote Sensing Applications: Society and Environment · Woo et al. 2026, Parasites & Vectors · Tarpenning et al. 2025, Parasites & Vectors · Rosser et al. 2024, Environmental Science and Pollution Research · Bramante et al. 2026, BMC Global and Public Health

title: Snail habitat, Brazil
text:
In July and August 2019 I flew drone surveys of ponds, streams and pastures at schistosomiasis study sites in southeastern Brazil, alongside snail sampling on the ground.
The wider Brazil work maps where the snails can live across the country, and how climate and growing cities are shifting that range, using satellite data and species models.



Papers: Glidden et al. 2024, Nature Communications · Singleton et al. 2024, PLOS Global Public Health · da Silva et al. 2024, PLOS NTD

title: Privacy
text:
This site
This site has no analytics, cookies or tracking scripts of its own. It is hosted on GitHub Pages, which keeps standard server logs, including IP addresses, under GitHub’s privacy statement.
The Photo & video page embeds YouTube videos in privacy-enhanced mode, which sets no YouTube cookies until you play a video; playback then falls under Google’s privacy policy. That page also loads its photo viewer from the jsDelivr CDN, which sees your IP address like any web host.

title: Privacy
text:
Map apps
The Earth Engine map apps linked from my project pages open without sign-in and collect nothing about you. Google runs them under its privacy policy.

title: Privacy
text:
Google sign-in
None of my public pages or apps ask you to sign in. Any tool of mine that uses Google sign-in is for my own account only, and its use of data from Google APIs follows the Google API Services User Data Policy, including the Limited Use requirements.
Questions: see the contact page.

title: Andy Chamberlin
text:
Drone and satellite mapping of landscapes and disease risk.
  



  I'm a research data scientist at Stanford. I use drones, satellites and deep learning to
  map ecological change across landscapes and pinpoint where disease risk is highest. I lead the
  drone and remote sensing work, from study design to finished maps, on projects in Senegal,
  Brazil, Costa Rica, Indonesia and Kenya. I also shoot and edit photo and video in the field.



  
    Drone mapping & spatial analysis
    Mosquito and snail habitat, vegetation and water mapping, crop monitoring, terrain and drainage.
  
  
    Satellite remote sensing & modeling
    Regional risk maps, habitat and species models, statistical modeling, and scaling drone results up to satellite.
  
  
    Computer vision & deep learning
    Custom models that find objects and map land cover in drone and satellite images, from labeled examples to finished maps.

title: About
text: I’m a research data scientist at Stanford University in Disease Ecology in a Changing World (DECO), a research initiative of the Stanford Center for Human and Planetary Health co-led by Giulio De Leo and Erin Mordecai. I also work closely with Joelle Rosser’s lab on dengue. I lead the drone and remote sensing work, from study design through published maps.

title: About
text:
What I do
I work across the whole arc of a project:

Shaping the questions and writing the grants
Designing studies and planning drone missions
Processing and calibrating drone and satellite imagery
Building computer vision models that pull features out of that imagery
Analysis and modeling
Presentations and papers

title: About
text:
Methods

Imagery: drone mapping, multispectral and spectral analysis, radiometric calibration, satellite imagery and Google Earth Engine
Terrain and water: elevation models, hydrological modeling and flow routing
Computer vision: deep learning to detect objects and map land cover, testing models in new places, scaling drone results up to satellite
Statistics: spatial statistics, machine learning, Bayesian inference, species distribution models
Tools: Python, R, QGIS, GPU model training on Stanford’s computing cluster

title: Forest canopy height, Borneo
text:
Canopy height is a good guide to how much carbon a forest holds and where it is being degraded. Measuring it usually takes airborne lidar, which is costly and covers only narrow strips.
I led a project that trained a deep learning model on lidar from 85 sites across Indonesian Borneo, paired with free satellite and terrain data. The model can predict canopy height at 30 m across Kalimantan wherever lidar is missing, and it was more accurate than the tree-based methods common in the field.



Forest loss. Building on the canopy height model, I mapped forest loss around villages in West Kalimantan for a study of how health care and livelihood programs held up during the pandemic.
Papers: Chamberlin et al. 2025, Remote Sensing · Hopkins et al. 2026, The Lancet Planetary Health
News: Stanford Woods Institute, July 2026

title: Rice and fish, Senegal
text:
Farmers in the Senegal River valley are testing fish in their rice fields: the fish eat the snails that carry schistosomiasis and can add income. The question for farmers is whether rice yield holds up.
I use drone and satellite imagery from the 2025 season to estimate yield field by field and to spot problems such as weeds, bare patches and uneven water. Partners in Senegal fly the drone surveys; I lead the analysis, from calibrating the imagery to the deep learning and statistical models that estimate yield and flag problem areas. Results will be shared once they’re published.
News: NPR, July 2026 · Stanford Report, January 2026

title: Snail habitat, Senegal
text:
Schistosomiasis spreads through freshwater snails that shelter in water plants. Since 2016 I have led drone mapping at village water sites along the lower Senegal River, flying the early surveys and later training local partners to fly them. The maps show how much of each site is open water and how much is covered by plants.
That plant cover turned out to predict how many children were infected better than counting snails did. It now guides where to remove plants and where to look for transmission.
Mapping plants by hand at every site doesn’t scale, so I’m building deep learning models that outline open water and floating and rooted plants in each drone map.
Papers: Wood et al. 2019, PNAS · Chamberlin et al. 2021, Geospatial Health · Jones et al. 2021, PLOS NTD · Liu et al. 2022, Remote Sensing
Video: Video abstract for Chamberlin et al. 2021
